prompt: Determine all composite integers $n > 1$ that satisfy the following property: if $d_1, d_2, \dots, d_k$ are all the positive divisors of $n$ with $1 = d_1 < d_2 < \dots < d_k = n$, then $d_i$ divides $d_{i+1} + d_{i+2}$ for every $1 \le i \le k-2$.
answer: Exactly the prime powers $n=p^r$ with $p$ prime and $r\ge2$.

solutions.title: Look at the largest divisors
solutions.body:
**Prime powers work.** If $n=p^r$ ($r\ge2$), the divisors are $d_i=p^{i-1}$, and $p^{i-1}\mid p^i+p^{i+1}$.

**Nothing else works.** Suppose $n$ has at least two prime factors; let $p<q$ be the two smallest. Let $p^e$ be the largest power of $p$ that divides $n$ and is less than $q$; $e\ge1$. Every divisor of $n$ smaller than $q$ has only prime factors smaller than $q$, i.e. it is a power of $p$; so the smallest divisors are
$$1<p<p^2<\dots<p^e<q.$$
Dividing $n$ by these, the largest divisors are
$$\frac nq<\frac n{p^e}<\frac n{p^{e-1}}<\dots<\frac np<n.$$
Apply the condition to $d_i=\frac nq$, whose two successors are $\frac n{p^e}$ and $\frac n{p^{e-1}}$:
$$\frac nq\ \Big|\ \frac n{p^e}+\frac n{p^{e-1}}=\frac{n(p+1)}{p^e}.$$
Hence $\dfrac{n(p+1)/p^e}{n/q}=\dfrac{q(p+1)}{p^e}$ is an integer. But $p\nmid q$ and $p\nmid p+1$, so $p\nmid q(p+1)$, while $e\ge1$, a contradiction.

**Answer:** $n=p^r$ for a prime $p$ and $r\ge2$.

prompt:
Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AB < AC$. Let $\Omega$ be the circumcircle of $ABC$. Let $S$ be the midpoint of the arc $CB$ of $\Omega$ containing $A$. The perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$ meets $BS$ at $D$ and meets $\Omega$ again at $E \ne A$. The line through $D$ parallel to $BC$ meets line $BE$ at $L$. Denote the circumcircle of triangle $BDL$ by $\omega$. Let $\omega$ meet $\Omega$ again at $P \ne B$.

Prove that the line tangent to $\omega$ at $P$ meets line $BS$ on the internal angle bisector of $\angle BAC$.
answer: Proof: $L,P,S$ and $P,D,F$ are collinear ($F$ the antipode of $A$); with $X=BS\cap AM$ ($M$ the arc midpoint), similar triangles give $XA=XY$ for $Y=PF\cap AM$, so $XP=XA$; an angle chase then shows $PX$ is tangent to $\omega$.

solutions.title: Antipode and a right triangle
solutions.body:
We use directed angles $\measuredangle$ modulo $180^\circ$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of arc $BC$ not containing $A$, so $AM$ is the bisector of $\angle BAC$, and $SM$ is a diameter of $\Omega$ perpendicular to $BC$. Let $F$ be the antipode of $A$; then $AMFS$ is a rectangle (both diagonals are diameters). Note $AE\perp BC$, so $AE\parallel SM$; and $\angle AEF=90^\circ$, so $EF\parallel BC\parallel DL$. Let $X=BS\cap AM$. We show that line $PX$ is tangent to $\omega$.

**$L,P,S$ are collinear.** Using $\omega$, $DL\parallel BC$, $SB=SC$ and $\Omega$:
$$\measuredangle LPB=\measuredangle LDB=\measuredangle CBD=\measuredangle CBS=\measuredangle SCB=\measuredangle SPB.$$

**$P,D,F$ are collinear.** The lines $AE$ (altitude) and $AF$ (through the circumcentre) are isogonal in $\angle A$, so $M$ is the midpoint of an arc $EF$; hence $E,F$ are symmetric in the diameter $SM$ and $SE=SF$. So line $BS$ bisects the angle between $BE$ and $BF$: $\measuredangle EBS=\measuredangle SBF$. Then
$$\measuredangle SPD=\measuredangle LPD=\measuredangle LBD=\measuredangle EBS=\measuredangle SBF=\measuredangle SPF.$$

**$XP=XA$.** Let $Y=PF\cap AM$ (so $D,Y,F,P$ are collinear). Since $AD\parallel MS$, triangles $AXD$ and $MXS$ are similar; since $XY\parallel SF$ (as $AM\parallel SF$), triangles $DXY$ and $DSF$ are similar. Hence
$$\frac{AX}{XD}=\frac{MX}{XS}=\frac{AX+XM}{XD+XS}=\frac{AM}{DS}=\frac{SF}{DS}=\frac{XY}{XD},$$
so $AX=XY$. As $AF$ is a diameter, $\angle APY=\angle APF=90^\circ$, so $X$ is the midpoint of the hypotenuse $AY$ of the right triangle $APY$, and $XP=XA$.

**Tangency.** From $XP=XA$, $\measuredangle XPA=\measuredangle PAX$, i.e. $\measuredangle(PX,PA)=\measuredangle PAM$. Also $\measuredangle APS=\measuredangle AMS=\measuredangle MAE$ (circle $\Omega$, then $MS\parallel AE$). So
$$\measuredangle(PX,PL)=\measuredangle(PX,PS)=\measuredangle(PX,PA)+\measuredangle APS=\measuredangle PAM+\measuredangle MAE=\measuredangle PAE.$$
Finally $\measuredangle PAE=\measuredangle PFE$ (circle $\Omega$) and, because $D$ lies on $PF$ and $EF\parallel DL$, $\measuredangle PFE=\measuredangle PDL$. Thus the angle between line $PX$ and the chord $PL$ of $\omega$ equals the inscribed angle $\measuredangle PDL$ on that chord; by the converse of the tangent–chord theorem, $PX$ is tangent to $\omega$ at $P$.

So the tangent at $P$ passes through $X$, which lies on $BS$ and on the bisector $AM$. ∎

prompt:
For each integer $k \ge 2$, determine all infinite sequences of positive integers $a_1, a_2, \dots$ for which there exists a polynomial $P$ of the form $P(x) = x^k + c_{k-1}x^{k-1} + \dots + c_1x + c_0$, where $c_0, c_1, \dots, c_{k-1}$ are non-negative integers, such that
$$P(a_n) = a_{n+1}a_{n+2}\cdots a_{n+k}$$
for every integer $n \ge 1$.
answer: Exactly the arithmetic progressions $a_n=a_1+(n-1)d$ with an integer $d\ge0$ (with $P(x)=(x+d)(x+2d)\cdots(x+kd)$).

solutions.title: Increasing, then compare with $(x+c_1)\cdots(x+c_k)$
solutions.body:
**These work.** If $a_n=a_1+(n-1)d$ with $d\ge0$, then $a_{n+1}\cdots a_{n+k}=(a_n+d)\cdots(a_n+kd)$, so $P(x)=(x+d)(x+2d)\cdots(x+kd)$ works (monic, non-negative integer coefficients).

Conversely let $(a_n)$ and $P$ satisfy the condition. Since $P$ has non-negative coefficients and is monic, it is strictly increasing on $[0,\infty)$.

**Eventually constant case.** If $a_n=\dots=a_{n+k}=c$ for some $n$, then $P(c)=c^k$, which forces $c_0=\dots=c_{k-1}=0$, i.e. $P(x)=x^k$. Then $P(a_{n-1})=a_n\cdots a_{n+k-1}=c^k$ gives $a_{n-1}=c$, and by backward induction the sequence is constant ($d=0$). So assume from now on that $(a_n)$ is not eventually constant.

**Step 1: $(a_n)$ is strictly increasing.** Dividing $P(a_{n+1})=a_{n+2}\cdots a_{n+k+1}$ by $P(a_n)=a_{n+1}\cdots a_{n+k}$ gives $\frac{P(a_{n+1})}{P(a_n)}=\frac{a_{n+k+1}}{a_{n+1}}$, so (as $P$ is increasing)
$$a_n<a_{n+1}\iff a_{n+1}<a_{n+k+1},\qquad a_n>a_{n+1}\iff a_{n+1}>a_{n+k+1},\qquad a_n=a_{n+1}\iff a_{n+1}=a_{n+k+1}.$$
*Non-decreasing.* Suppose $a_{m-1}>a_m$ for some $m=m_0$. Given $m_i$ with $a_{m_i-1}>a_{m_i}$, we have $a_{m_i}>a_{m_i+k}$, so there is a smallest index $m_{i+1}\in(m_i,m_i+k]$ with $a_{m_{i+1}}<a_{m_i}$. Then also $a_{m_{i+1}-1}>a_{m_{i+1}}$ (if $m_{i+1}-1>m_i$, minimality gives $a_{m_{i+1}-1}\ge a_{m_i}$). This produces an infinite strictly decreasing sequence $a_{m_0}>a_{m_1}>\cdots$ of positive integers, impossible.
*Strict.* If $a_n=a_{n+1}$, then $a_{n+1}=a_{n+k+1}$ and by monotonicity $a_n=\dots=a_{n+k+1}$; repeating from $a_{n+k}=a_{n+k+1}$ shows the sequence is eventually constant, excluded. So $a_n<a_{n+1}$ for all $n$; in particular $a_n\to\infty$.

**Step 2: the sum of differences is the coefficient $b=c_{k-1}$.** Write
$$P(a_n)=(a_n+e_1)(a_n+e_2)\cdots(a_n+e_k),\qquad e_i=a_{n+i}-a_n\ge1.$$
For a tuple $c=(c_1,\dots,c_k)$ of positive integers, $P(x)-\prod(x+c_i)=(b-\sum c_i)x^{k-1}+(\text{lower terms})$. There is a bound $A$ such that for all $x\ge A$:
- if $\sum c_i>b$ then $P(x)<\prod(x+c_i)$: take $A$ working for the finitely many tuples with $\sum c_i=b+1$; any tuple with larger sum dominates one of these entrywise;
- if $\sum c_i<b$ then $P(x)>\prod(x+c_i)$: there are finitely many such tuples.

For $n$ large, $a_n\ge A$, so the tuple $(e_1,\dots,e_k)$ must have $\sum_i(a_{n+i}-a_n)=b$. Subtracting this equation for $n$ from the one for $n+1$:
$$a_{n+k+1}-a_{n+1}=k(a_{n+1}-a_n)\qquad\text{for all large }n.$$

**Step 3: constant differences.** Let $d$ be the minimum of $a_{n+1}-a_n$ over large $n$, attained at $n_0$. Then
$$kd=a_{n_0+k+1}-a_{n_0+1}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}(a_{n_0+i+1}-a_{n_0+i}),$$
a sum of $k$ terms each $\ge d$, so all equal $d$. Inductively every difference from $n_0$ on equals $d$. Then $P(a_n)=(a_n+d)\cdots(a_n+kd)$ for infinitely many values $a_n$, so $P(x)=(x+d)(x+2d)\cdots(x+kd)$.

**Backward induction.** If $a_n,\dots,a_{n+k}$ is an arithmetic progression with difference $d$, then $P(a_{n-1})=a_n\cdots a_{n+k-1}=P(a_n-d)$; $P$ is strictly increasing on $(-d,\infty)$ and both $a_{n-1}$ and $a_n-d$ lie there, so $a_{n-1}=a_n-d$. Hence the whole sequence is an arithmetic progression with difference $d\ge1$.

**Answer:** exactly the arithmetic progressions of positive integers with non-negative common difference. ∎

prompt:
Let $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{2023}$ be pairwise different positive real numbers such that
$$a_n = \sqrt{(x_1 + x_2 + \dots + x_n)\left(\frac{1}{x_1} + \frac{1}{x_2} + \dots + \frac{1}{x_n}\right)}$$
is an integer for every $n = 1, 2, \dots, 2023$. Prove that $a_{2023} \ge 3034$.
answer: Proof: Cauchy–Schwarz gives $a_{n+2}\ge a_n+\sqrt{x_{n+1}/x_{n+2}}+\sqrt{x_{n+2}/x_{n+1}}>a_n+2$, so $a_{n+2}\ge a_n+3$; with $a_1=1$ this gives $a_{2023}\ge1+3\cdot1011=3034$.

solutions.title: Cauchy–Schwarz two steps at a time
solutions.body:
Clearly $a_1=1$. We show $a_{n+2}\ge a_n+3$ for $1\le n\le2021$; then $a_{2m+1}\ge 3m+1$ and in particular $a_{2023}\ge 3\cdot1011+1=3034$.

Fix $n$ and let $s=x_1+\dots+x_n$, $t=\frac1{x_1}+\dots+\frac1{x_n}$, so $a_n^2=st$; let $p=x_{n+1}$, $q=x_{n+2}$. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, pairing $s$ with $t$, $p$ with $\frac1q$, and $q$ with $\frac1p$:
$$a_{n+2}^2=(s+p+q)\Big(t+\frac1q+\frac1p\Big)\ge\Big(\sqrt{st}+\sqrt{\tfrac pq}+\sqrt{\tfrac qp}\Big)^2.$$
With $u=\sqrt{p/q}$, this says $a_{n+2}\ge a_n+u+\frac1u$. Since $p\ne q$, $u\ne1$ and $u+\frac1u>2$ (AM–GM, strict). So $a_{n+2}>a_n+2$, and as both are integers, $a_{n+2}\ge a_n+3$. ∎

prompt:
Let $n$ be a positive integer. A *Japanese triangle* consists of $1 + 2 + \dots + n$ circles arranged in an equilateral triangular shape such that for each $i = 1, 2, \dots, n$, the $i$-th row contains exactly $i$ circles, exactly one of which is coloured red. A *ninja path* in a Japanese triangle is a sequence of $n$ circles obtained by starting in the top row, then repeatedly going from a circle to one of the two circles immediately below it and finishing in the bottom row. The picture shows an example of a Japanese triangle with $n = 6$, along with a ninja path in that triangle containing two red circles.

In terms of $n$, find the greatest $k$ such that in each Japanese triangle there is a ninja path containing at least $k$ red circles.

solutions.title: Construction in blocks of rows, and row sums
solutions.body:
Let $N=\lfloor\log_2n\rfloor$, so $2^N\le n<2^{N+1}$. Number the circles of row $i$ as $1,\dots,i$ from the left; from circle $j$ in row $i$ a path goes to circle $j$ or $j+1$ in row $i+1$.

**Construction with at most $N+1$.** For row $i=2^a+b$ with $0\le b<2^a$, colour circle $2b+1$ red (note $2b+1\le 2^a+b$). Suppose a path met red circles in two rows $2^a+b<2^a+b'$ of the same block $\{2^a,\dots,2^{a+1}-1\}$. Its position grows by at most $1$ per row, so in row $2^a+b'$ it is at most $(2b+1)+(b'-b)=b+b'+1<2b'+1$, a contradiction. So each path meets at most one red circle per block, and rows $1,\dots,n$ meet the $N+1$ blocks $a=0,\dots,N$: at most $N+1$ red circles.

**Every triangle has a path with $N+1$.** Give each circle $C$ the value $v(C)$ = the largest number of red circles on a path from the top to $C$ (inclusive). If $C$ has parent(s) above it, $v(C)$ is the maximum over its parents, plus $1$ if $C$ is red.

Let $v_1,\dots,v_i$ be the values in row $i$, with maximum $v_m$, and $\sigma_i$ their sum. In row $i+1$, circle $j\le m$ has parent $j$ and circle $j\ge m+1$ has parent $j-1$, so the values in row $i+1$ are at least $v_1,\dots,v_m,v_m,v_{m+1},\dots,v_i$, and the red circle gets $1$ more. Hence
$$\sigma_{i+1}\ge\sigma_i+v_m+1=\sigma_i+\max(\text{row }i)+1.$$
Also the row maximum never decreases from one row to the next.

*Claim:* $\sigma_{2^j}\ge j\cdot2^j+1$ for $0\le j\le N$. For $j=0$, $\sigma_1=1$ (the top circle is red). If it holds for $j<N$, the maximum in row $2^j$ is at least $\lceil\sigma_{2^j}/2^j\rceil\ge j+1$, hence so is the maximum of every later row, and
$$\sigma_{2^{j+1}}\ge\sigma_{2^j}+2^j(j+2)\ge j2^j+1+(j+2)2^j=(j+1)2^{j+1}+1.$$

For $j=N$, some circle of row $2^N\le n$ has value at least $\lceil (N2^N+1)/2^N\rceil=N+1$, i.e. some path from the top to it contains $N+1$ red circles; continue it arbitrarily to the bottom row.

**Answer:** $k=\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor+1$.

prompt:
Let $ABC$ be an equilateral triangle. Let $A_1, B_1, C_1$ be interior points of $ABC$ such that $BA_1 = A_1C$, $CB_1 = B_1A$, $AC_1 = C_1B$, and
$$\angle BA_1C + \angle CB_1A + \angle AC_1B = 480^\circ.$$
Let $BC_1$ and $CB_1$ meet at $A_2$, let $CA_1$ and $AC_1$ meet at $B_2$, and let $AB_1$ and $BA_1$ meet at $C_2$.

Prove that if triangle $A_1B_1C_1$ is scalene, then the three circumcircles of triangles $AA_1A_2$, $BB_1B_2$ and $CC_1C_2$ all pass through two common points.

(Note: a scalene triangle is one where no two sides have equal length.)
answer: Proof: $A_1$ is the circumcentre of $A_2BC$ (etc.), which makes $B_1C_1B_2C_2$, $C_1A_1C_2A_2$, $A_1B_1A_2B_2$ cyclic; each circle of the problem is a locus $\mathrm{Pow}(P,\omega)=k\,\mathrm{Pow}(P,\omega')$ for two of these, with $k_ak_bk_c=1$, so a common point of two of them lies on the third; the crossing of the diagonals $A_1A_2$, $B_1B_2$ shows that two of them do meet twice.

solutions.title: Coaxal circles via ratios of powers
solutions.body:
Let $O$ be the centre of $ABC$ and put
$$\alpha=\angle A_1BC=\angle A_1CB,\qquad\beta=\angle B_1CA=\angle B_1AC,\qquad\gamma=\angle C_1AB=\angle C_1BA.$$
Then $\angle BA_1C=180^\circ-2\alpha$ etc., and the angle condition becomes $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=30^\circ$. So each of $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ is less than $30^\circ$ and $\angle BA_1C>120^\circ=\angle BOC$: $A_1$ lies inside triangle $BOC$, and similarly $B_1$ in $COA$, $C_1$ in $AOB$. From this one sees that $C_1$ lies between $B$ and $A_2$ (and the analogous statements), and that the hexagon $A_2C_1B_2A_1C_2B_1$ is convex.

**Step 1: $A_1$ is the circumcentre of $A_2BC$.** We have $\angle CBA_2=\angle CBC_1=60^\circ-\gamma$ and $\angle BCA_2=60^\circ-\beta$, so
$$\angle BA_2C=60^\circ+\beta+\gamma=90^\circ-\alpha=\tfrac12\angle BA_1C.$$
As $A_1$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $BC$, on the same side as $A_2$, it is the circumcentre of $BA_2C$. Likewise $B_1$ is the circumcentre of $CB_2A$ and $C_1$ of $AC_2B$.

**Step 2: three auxiliary circles.** With directed angles: $C_2$ lies on line $AB_1$, and $B_1$ is the centre of circle $(AB_2C)$, so $\measuredangle(B_1B_2,B_1C_2)=-\measuredangle(B_1A,B_1B_2)=-2\measuredangle(CA,CA_1)$. Similarly $B_2$ lies on line $AC_1$ and $C_1$ is the centre of $(AC_2B)$, so $\measuredangle(C_1B_2,C_1C_2)=2\measuredangle(BA,BA_1)$. By the symmetry of $A_1$ in the perpendicular bisector of $BC$, $\measuredangle(BA,BA_1)=-\measuredangle(CA,CA_1)$. Hence $\measuredangle B_2B_1C_2=\measuredangle B_2C_1C_2$ and
$$\omega_a:=(B_1C_1B_2C_2),\qquad\omega_b:=(C_1A_1C_2A_2),\qquad\omega_c:=(A_1B_1A_2B_2)$$
are circles (the last two by the same argument). They are pairwise distinct: if two coincided, all six points would lie on one circle, and the convex hexagon $A_2C_1B_2A_1C_2B_1$ would be cyclic, so its angles at $A_1,B_1,C_1$ would add up to $360^\circ$. But those angles are the vertical angles $\angle BA_1C,\angle CB_1A,\angle AC_1B$, whose sum is $480^\circ$.

**Step 3: the circle $(AA_1A_2)$ as a locus.** $\omega_b$ and $\omega_c$ both pass through $A_1,A_2$. Let line $AA_1$ meet $\omega_c$ again at $X$ and $\omega_b$ again at $Y$ (both between $A$ and $A_1$), and set $k_a=\frac{AX}{AY}$. For any constant $k$, the set of points $P$ with $\mathrm{Pow}(P,\omega_c)=k\,\mathrm{Pow}(P,\omega_b)$ is a circle if $k\ne1$ and the radical axis if $k=1$ (in coordinates, $\mathrm{Pow}((x,y),\omega)=x^2+y^2+(\text{linear})$). For $k=k_a$ this set contains $A_1$ and $A_2$ (both powers $0$) and $A$ (since $\mathrm{Pow}(A,\omega_c)=AX\cdot AA_1$ and $\mathrm{Pow}(A,\omega_b)=AY\cdot AA_1$).

*Computing $k_a$.* $X\in\omega_c$, so $\angle A_1XB_1=\angle A_1B_2B_1=\angle CB_2B_1$; since $B_1$ is the centre of $(CB_2A)$, the isosceles triangle $B_1CB_2$ gives $\angle CB_2B_1=90^\circ-\angle CAB_2=90^\circ-(60^\circ-\gamma)=30^\circ+\gamma$. In triangle $AXB_1$, $\angle XAB_1=\angle A_1AC-\angle B_1AC=30^\circ-\beta$, and $\angle A_1XB_1$ is the exterior angle at $X$, so $\angle AB_1X=(30^\circ+\gamma)-(30^\circ-\beta)=\beta+\gamma$. The law of sines gives
$$AX=AB_1\frac{\sin(\beta+\gamma)}{\sin(30^\circ+\gamma)},\qquad\text{and similarly}\qquad AY=AC_1\frac{\sin(\beta+\gamma)}{\sin(30^\circ+\beta)}.$$
With $AB_1=\frac{s}{2\cos\beta}$, $AC_1=\frac{s}{2\cos\gamma}$ ($s$ the side length) and $g(t)=\frac{\sin(30^\circ+t)}{\cos t}$,
$$k_a=\frac{g(\beta)}{g(\gamma)}.$$
The function $g$ is strictly increasing on $[0^\circ,30^\circ]$, and $\beta\ne\gamma$ because $A_1B_1\ne A_1C_1$ (if $\beta=\gamma$ the figure is symmetric in line $AA_1$). So $k_a\ne1$, the locus is a genuine circle through $A,A_1,A_2$, and it is the circumcircle $\delta_A=(AA_1A_2)$.

By the same computation (cyclically),
$$\delta_A:\ \mathrm{Pow}(P,\omega_c)=k_a\mathrm{Pow}(P,\omega_b),\quad \delta_B:\ \mathrm{Pow}(P,\omega_a)=k_b\mathrm{Pow}(P,\omega_c),\quad \delta_C:\ \mathrm{Pow}(P,\omega_b)=k_c\mathrm{Pow}(P,\omega_a),$$
with $k_b=\frac{g(\gamma)}{g(\alpha)}$, $k_c=\frac{g(\alpha)}{g(\beta)}$, so $k_ak_bk_c=1$.

**Step 4: common points.** If $P\in\delta_A\cap\delta_B$, then $\mathrm{Pow}(P,\omega_a)=k_ak_b\,\mathrm{Pow}(P,\omega_b)$, i.e. $\mathrm{Pow}(P,\omega_b)=k_c\,\mathrm{Pow}(P,\omega_a)$, so $P\in\delta_C$. It remains to show that $\delta_A$ and $\delta_B$ meet in two points.

In the convex hexagon $A_2C_1B_2A_1C_2B_1$ the diagonals $A_1A_2$ and $B_1B_2$ cross at a point $Z$ interior to both. Then $\mathrm{Pow}(Z,\delta_A)=-ZA_1\cdot ZA_2$ and $\mathrm{Pow}(Z,\delta_B)=-ZB_1\cdot ZB_2$; both equal $\mathrm{Pow}(Z,\omega_c)$ because $A_1,A_2,B_1,B_2\in\omega_c$. So $Z$ has the same negative power with respect to $\delta_A$ and $\delta_B$. (If $\delta_A=\delta_B$, all three circles coincide by the previous paragraph and there is nothing to prove.) Otherwise $\delta_A,\delta_B$ are not concentric (concentric circles never give equal powers), and $Z$ lies on their radical axis. Since $Z$ is inside $\delta_A$, this line meets $\delta_A$ at two points; they have power $0$ with respect to $\delta_A$, hence also with respect to $\delta_B$, and then they lie on $\delta_C$ too. ∎
